title: Detection of Malware
summary: This detection strategy covers the technique of obtaining malware, where an adversary buys, downloads, or receives an existing malicious payload instead of writing one. It matters because the payload is the part of the intrusion that runs on your systems, so its first landing is often the earliest solid evidence you get. The telemetry that makes detection possible is endpoint detection and response alerts, file creation and hash records, sandbox analysis results, and network records of contact with known distribution or command servers. The main failure mode is that unknown samples have no hash history, so the rule depends on behaviour and reputation and must tolerate a steady stream of low confidence alerts.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for malicious software that arrives on your systems. Malicious software, or malware, is a program written to harm or control a computer. The rule watches files as they are written and checks what they try to do. It catches downloads from sources that are known to be bad.
beginner.whyItMatters: Malware is the part of an attack that actually runs. If you catch the file early, the rest of the attack may never start. Some malware is bought finished, so it looks the same on many victims. Watching where files come from links the sample to the wider campaign.
howItWorks: The endpoint agent watches every file written to disk and records its hash.
Brand new hashes are sent to a sandbox, which runs the file and reports what it does.
The rule checks hashes and file behaviour against threat intelligence sources.
Network logs show contacts with addresses that are known to deliver or control malware.
The SIEM joins the file record to the process that created it and the user account.
A match on reputation, or behaviour such as process injection, raises a high priority alert.
beginner.example: Picture a post room where every parcel is weighed and x rayed. Most parcels are ordinary supplies and pass through. One parcel ticks in the same way as a known bad item. Another comes from an address on the warning list. Both are opened in a safe room. The post room log is our file and network record.
takeaways: Behaviour and reputation carry the detection when the hash is new.
Joining file records to process and user records turns a sample into an incident.
Bought malware is reused across victims, so shared indicators help even before analysis.

objectives: Explain why obtaining malware is a distinct and observable step.
Name the endpoint, sandbox, and network records that support this detection.
Write a rule that combines reputation matches with suspicious file behaviour.
Describe how to triage a new sample with no hash history.
Identify the operational limits of signature based detection.
dataSources: Endpoint detection and response alert records with process, file hash and behaviour classification
Antivirus file scan and quarantine records including file path and detection name
Network proxy and firewall logs showing contact with known malware distribution or command and control addresses
Malware sandbox analysis reports for new samples submitted from managed endpoints
logic: The pattern is a file that lands on a managed host and matches a known malicious hash or shows behaviour that only malicious tooling performs, such as writing a run key and injecting into another process, or an endpoint talking to an address observed delivering payloads. The fields that must be correlated are the file hash and path, the creating process and its parent, the user account, the execution behaviour, and any matching network destination. The distinguishing detail is a combination of a new or low reputation file with behaviour or network contact that a normal business tool does not produce. The benign case is signed administrative tooling that the security team itself runs, which behaves similarly but comes from an approved source.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Newly Written File With Malicious Reputation or Behaviour
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: sysmon
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 11
#     FileName|endswith:
#       - '.exe'
#       - '.dll'
#       - '.scr'
#   filter_signed:
#     SignatureStatus: 'Valid'
#     Signature|contains: 'Organization Name'
#   condition: selection and not filter_signed
# level: high
falsePositives: Security operations staff running penetration testing or forensic utilities that trigger malicious behaviour rules
Software deployment tools that push unsigned installers and scripts from an internal management share
Backup and remote support agents that inject code into other processes for legitimate monitoring
tuningNotes: Start by allow listing the signed administrative and security tools your own teams use, and filter valid signatures from publishers you have approved, so the rule focuses on unsigned or newly signed files. Scope hash based alerts to endpoints, and route sandbox only traffic to a separate queue so it does not bury behaviour alerts. The coverage you lose is a signed payload that abuses a stolen certificate, and hash matching fails against a fresh sample, so keep behaviour rules and network contact rules running alongside this one.
